issues.legal_issue: A person who advances purchase money under an agreement to acquire a share in property may obtain that share even if the purchaser initially bid and paid the deposit alone.
material_facts: The purchaser bid for the property and paid the auction deposits himself before the other participants provided money.
Two participants each paid money toward completion of the purchase, and the purchaser acknowledged receiving those payments.
The purchaser signed an agreement providing for equal shares and applied to have the conveyance made jointly, although the conveyance was ultimately made to him alone.
The evidence did not establish that the payments were loans; the court inferred that they were made in return for shares in the property.
The two contributing participants did not prove payment of their additional share of expenses, while the third participant did not prove any contribution.
The purchaser had collected rent from the property.
issues.conclusion: The two participants who contributed toward the purchase were entitled to a one-fourth share each, subject to paying their respective shares of the expenses, and to their shares of the rent collected. The participant who proved no contribution was entitled to no relief.
issues.legal_principle: On the evidence as a whole, payments made toward acquiring property in return for an agreed share are not merely loans, and the agreed share may be enforced. The court found that the agreement was not shown to have resulted from undue influence. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on in deciding this issue.

rule.if: suit_claims_beneficial_co_ownership_after_property_purchase and purchaser_initially_bid_and_paid_alone and contributors_paid_toward_purchase and purchaser_agreed_to_share_property and payments_were_for_shares_not_loans

predicates.suit_claims_beneficial_co_ownership_afte: A claimant brought a suit asserting beneficial co-ownership and seeking a share of property acquired through a purchase.
predicates.purchaser_initially_bid_and_paid_alone: The person in whose name the purchase was made placed the bid and paid the initial deposit without contributions from the other claimants.
predicates.contributors_paid_toward_purchase: Other claimants provided money that was used toward completing the purchase.
predicates.purchaser_agreed_to_share_property: The purchaser signed an agreement to share the property and sought a conveyance in the participants' joint names.
predicates.payments_were_for_shares_not_loans: The evidence showed that the money was provided in return for shares in the property rather than as a loan.

issues.definition: When a co-ownership suit follows a purchase initially funded by the named purchaser alone, contributors who later paid toward the purchase under an agreement for shares are entitled to those shares, subject to their share of expenses.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory bar on suits alleging that a court-certified purchase was made on behalf of another person does not apply to a property sale conducted by a court-appointed receiver.
material_facts: The property was sold through a receiver appointed by the court.
The receiver conveyed the property to the purchaser under the applicable court rules.
The conveyance was not a certificate issued under the procedure for court execution sales of immovable property.
The claimants alleged beneficial ownership based on the assertion that the purchase was made for them as well as for the named purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The statutory bar did not apply because the sale was conducted by a receiver and was not a sale for which the prescribed court certificate was issued.
issues.legal_principle: Section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to a purchase certified by the court in the prescribed manner. The relevant prescribed certificate is the certificate contemplated by Order 21, Rule 94, following confirmation of an execution sale under Order 21, Rule 92. A receiver's sale under Order 40, Rule 1, is not such an execution sale, so Section 66 does not apply. The court relied on the text of those provisions and distinguished the Privy Council decision in Bishun Dayal v. Kesho Prasad, which concerned a claim based on an auction purchase governed by Section 66.

predicates.suit_claims_purchase_was_for_another_per: A claimant brought a suit alleging that a purchase made in another person's name was made on the claimant's behalf.
predicates.property_sold_by_court_appointed_receive: A court-appointed receiver conducted the property sale.
predicates.no_prescribed_execution_sale_certificate: The purchaser did not receive the certificate prescribed for a court execution sale of immovable property.

issues.definition: The statutory bar does not apply when a claimant alleges that a purchase was made on the claimant's behalf but the property was sold by a court-appointed receiver without the prescribed execution-sale certificate.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered agreement cannot by itself displace title conveyed to another person, but it does not make a suit based on an independent claim of real ownership unmaintainable.
material_facts: The property was conveyed to the purchaser alone through a registered conveyance.
The claimants relied in part on an unregistered agreement concerning their asserted shares.
The suit also asserted that the property had been acquired in co-ownership and that the claimants were its real owners.
The registration objection was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court, and the court permitted it to be argued as a pure question of law.
issues.conclusion: The claimants could not displace the purchaser's title on the unregistered agreement alone, but the objection did not require dismissal of the suit because the claim of real ownership was not based on that agreement alone.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory requirement that an interest be created by a registered instrument cannot be overridden by applying an English equitable doctrine to create that interest without the required writing. The court relied on G.H.C. Ariff v. Jadunath Majumdar Bahadur and Maritime Electric Co. Ltd. v. General Dairies Ltd. It nevertheless distinguished a claim of real ownership that is not founded solely on the unregistered agreement.

rule.if: suit_claims_real_ownership and claim_relies_on_bases_beyond_unregistered_agreement and title_was_conveyed_to_another_person and agreement_was_unregistered

predicates.suit_claims_real_ownership: A claimant brought a suit asserting that the claimant was a real owner of the property.
predicates.claim_relies_on_bases_beyond_unregistere: The claim of ownership was supported by grounds other than the unregistered agreement.
predicates.title_was_conveyed_to_another_person: A conveyance of the property placed title in a person other than the claimant.
predicates.agreement_was_unregistered: The agreement relied on to assert an interest in the property was not registered.

issues.definition: An unregistered agreement cannot alone defeat another person's conveyed title, but a claimant's independent real-ownership claim is not unmaintainable merely because the claimant also relies on that agreement.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may permit a new pure question of law to be raised for the first time when deciding it requires no investigation of facts.
material_facts: A party raised an objection for the first time in the Supreme Court.
The objection was a pure question of law and did not require investigation of facts.
The court permitted the party to argue the objection.
issues.conclusion: The court permitted the new legal objection to be raised because it involved no investigation of facts.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law that does not require factual investigation may be raised for the first time in an appellate court. The court relied on Yaswant Deorao Deshmukh v. Walchand Ramchand Kothari, Raja Sri Sailendra Narayan Bhanja Deo v. State of Orissa, Seth Badri Prasad v. Seth Nagarmal, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Anand Swarup, and T.G. Appanda Mudaliar v. State of Madras.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party raised the ground while a court was hearing an appeal.
predicates.new_ground_raises_pure_question_of_law: The ground had not been raised in the courts below and presented a pure question of law.
predicates.deciding_ground_requires_no_factual_inve: The court could decide the ground without investigating facts.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a new ground may be considered when it presents a pure question of law that requires no factual investigation.
